## Wooden Rails Below Ground

The railway began as a way of moving heavy loads over short distances, and its first home was underground. In the mines of late medieval and early modern Europe, carts hauling ore and coal along muddy galleries wore out wheels, stalled in soft ground, and needed several men to push them. Miners began laying timber boards or planks along the route so that the wheels ran on a smoother, firmer surface. Once the timber wore, they replaced it with a second, sturdier layer, and the arrangement became recognizable as a track.

Georgius Agricola's *De re metallica*, published in 1556, shows this practice in a German mining district. The illustrations include small wagons running on timber rails, with the wheels guided by the rails and the cart's load pushed by hand. Such wagonways were not new to Agricola's readers, which suggests the method was already common in the German and Bohemian mining regions by the early sixteenth century. What the book did was describe the technique in print, so it could travel to other places where mines needed the same solution.

England's wagonways developed on a similar logic. The coalfields of the north-east, around Newcastle and along the Tyne and Wear, were the most important of these. Coal was dug far from the rivers, and getting it to the staithes where it could be loaded onto ships meant moving tens of thousands of tons over distances of several miles. Horses pulled the wagons along timber rails, usually with a single horse hitched to a set of linked wagons. Some of the earliest English wagonways date from the early seventeenth century. The Wollaton wagonway near Nottingham, built around 1604 for a coal mine owned by the Beaumont family, is often cited as one of the first, though records of such early lines are thin and historians disagree about which should be called the first.

These wagonways had a basic structure that would persist for two centuries. The track was a pair of parallel rails. The wagon had flanged wheels or the rail had a flange, and the flanges kept the vehicle on course. The rails were laid to a fixed width, the gauge, which was set by the wagons the owners already possessed rather than by any general plan. This local, practical origin mattered later, because the gauge of a wagonway determined what could run on it, and each colliery had its own customs. Wagonways were private, built by owners for their own purposes, and they connected a single mine or group of mines to a river, a canal, or a port. Nobody thought of them as a network. They were pieces of industrial equipment, and they were expensive to lay and maintain.

## Iron Rails and the Horse Tramroad

Timber rails had obvious weaknesses. They wore quickly under heavy loads, they rotted, and they splintered. From the middle of the eighteenth century, ironmasters began experimenting with iron. The advantage was durability, and the iron industry had reached a scale where it could supply large quantities of material cheaply enough.

The decisive experiments took place in Shropshire, in the Severn Gorge around Coalbrookdale. Abraham Darby III, whose family had pioneered the use of coke in iron smelting, cast iron rails in the 1760s and laid them for a tramway serving the works. Cast iron was brittle, and early rails were prone to breaking, so the design evolved. Iron plates were made with flanges on the inside, forming what became known as a plateway. The wheels ran on the flat top of the plate while the flange sat on the inside of the rail, and in some systems the flange was on the wheel instead. These were the early tramways, and the word "tramroad" came to describe lines of this kind.

Benjamin Outram, an engineer who worked on several of the early tramroads, gave his name to the "outram" which was soon shortened to "tramway." He built lines in Derbyshire and elsewhere, and his work with the Butterley Company helped establish iron tramroads as a reliable form of infrastructure. Josias Jessop built the Cromford and High Peak Railway, which opened in the early 1830s, using a combination of level stretches, inclined planes worked by stationary engines and cable, and horse haulage. It was a substantial piece of engineering, showing that the tramroad could handle a serious gradient if the design was adapted to suit.

The most important of these early iron lines in terms of public significance was the Surrey Iron Railway, which opened in 1803 between Wandsworth and Croydon, south of London. It is generally described as the first public railway: it was built under an Act of Parliament, it was open to any carrier who paid a toll for using the track, and horses and wagons from many operators ran over it. This is the crucial conceptual step. A wagonway served its owner. A public railway served the general market, with a separation between the owner of the track and the operators of the vehicles. The Surrey Iron Railway was a toll road in iron, and the idea that infrastructure could be shared, paid for by tolls, and open to many users would shape railway law for the rest of the century.

Horse-drawn tramroads were also cheap enough to spread. By the early nineteenth century, a web of iron tramways connected coal and iron districts across Britain. Their significance is that they accustomed engineers, investors, and workers to the idea of a track as a long-lived, load-bearing investment, and they made the problems of gauge, gradient, and wear into matters of routine practice. When steam arrived, it was grafted onto this infrastructure.

## Steam Reaches the Rails

Steam power predated the railway by a long time. Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine, built from the 1710s, pumped water out of mines using a cylinder, a piston, and condensing steam. It was heavy, slow, and inefficient in its use of fuel, but it worked, and it was used across the coalfields. James Watt's separate condenser, patented in 1769 and developed with Matthew Boulton, greatly improved efficiency by keeping the cylinder hot and condensing steam in a separate vessel. Watt's engines were expensive and were initially applied to pumping and then to driving machinery in factories. Mechanical power through rotary motion came later, through the sun-and-planet gear Watt designed to convert reciprocating motion into rotation.

The idea of a steam carriage was older than either. Several inventors built road locomotives in the late eighteenth century, but the difficulties were formidable. Boilers were heavy and fragile, adhesion on rails was thought to be insufficient, and a locomotive had to carry its own fuel and water. Richard Trevithick, a Cornish engineer who had worked on high-pressure steam engines, built a road locomotive in 1801 and then turned to rail. In 1804 he built a locomotive for the Penydarren ironworks in South Wales. On 21 February 1804 it made a run along the tramroad from Penydarren to Abercynon, a distance of about nine miles, pulling a load of around ten tons of iron and, according to the account, seventy men riding on the wagons. The run was a demonstration rather than a commercial service. The cast-iron plateway proved too weak for the engine's weight, and some rails broke. Trevithick did not pursue the project, and the locomotive was not put into regular use. Still, it showed that a steam engine could pull a train, and the demonstration was widely reported.

The problem Trevithick had run into was adhesion and track strength. Two early solutions tried to address the first. John Blenkinsop, manager of the Middleton Colliery near Leeds, patented a locomotive in 1811 that used a toothed wheel meshing with a rack laid alongside one of the rails. The idea was that the rack would give the wheel grip, so the engine could pull heavy loads without slipping. Matthew Murray built Blenkinsop's engines, and the Middleton Railway began regular working with them in 1812. The rack was unnecessary in principle, because later experiments showed that smooth wheels could grip a smooth rail well enough, but at the time the rack seemed prudent. Blenkinsop's engines were the first steam locomotives to run in regular commercial service.

William Hedley's *Puffing Billy*, built for the Wylam Colliery near Newcastle around 1813 and 1814, used smooth wheels on the rails, and it worked. Hedley's engines and those of Christopher Blackett, the colliery owner, were practical machines that suggested steam haulage could work on the basic plateway. At the same colliery, a young engineer named George Stephenson was learning the trade. Stephenson had worked as a brakeman and then as an engineman on the Killingworth colliery's engines, and he built his first locomotive, *Blücher*, in 1814 for the Killingworth wagonway. *Blücher* was an engine with smooth wheels, and it proved that Stephenson could build steam locomotives that worked reliably on a relatively light track.

Stephenson's competitors and collaborators are important to the story. Timothy Hackworth, who worked for the Stockton and Darlington, was an able locomotive builder and a fierce partisan of the steam engine. Hackworth's *Sans Pareil* would later compete at Rainhill. Stephenson's son Robert, who studied in Edinburgh and worked in Colombia, returned to England to become a partner in the family firm, which would build a great many of the engines of the next generation. The people who worked in these small firms and colliery yards formed the human base from which the railway emerged, and their practical knowledge of metallurgy, boilers, and gradients was more important than any one patent.

## The Stockton, the Darlington, and Locomotion Number One

The Stockton and Darlington Railway, authorised by Parliament in 1821 and opened on 27 September 1825, is often called the world's first public steam railway. This description needs some care. The line was built as a railway for the carriage of coal, and it was authorised as a public railway open to carriers on payment of tolls. Horses hauled much of the traffic, and the company's first plans did not envisage steam locomotives as the main form of power. George Stephenson persuaded the directors to use steam, and he built *Locomotion Number One* for the opening. The engine hauled a train that included coal wagons and a number of carriages carrying passengers, and on the opening day several hundred people travelled on the line, some riding in wagons that had been fitted with seats.

The Stockton and Darlington was not a quick or elegant line. Its route included a long, awkward climb and a number of inclines worked by stationary engines, and steam locomotives were used for part of the route rather than all of it. Even so, the line proved that steam could work in regular commercial operation, and it gave the Stephensons a reputation and a template. Stephenson's engineers had also learned how to lay track on a route that needed to be level and to cope with the difficulties of ground that was unstable or waterlogged.

The Stockton and Darlington attracted visitors and imitators, and the idea that a railway could carry both goods and people caught on. The period after 1825 saw a growing awareness that the railway might be more than a colliery tool. Investors began to consider the possibility of lines between major towns, and the engineering problems of such lines were far greater than those of a coal line. The big question was whether a steam railway could compete with canals, turnpike roads, and coastal shipping, and whether the market for passenger travel would justify the capital cost.

## The Rainhill Trials and the Liverpool and Manchester

The Liverpool and Manchester Railway was the line that answered many of these questions. Liverpool was the port through which much of the raw cotton for Manchester's mills arrived, and the route between the two cities was crowded with canal and road traffic. Parliament authorised the line in 1826 after a difficult contest with canal interests and landowners. The engineering was hard. The line had to cross Chat Moss, a large peat bog, and the route required cuttings, embankments, and bridges. George Stephenson was appointed engineer, and the work was carried out largely under his direction.

The directors were not sure that locomotives were the best way to haul trains on the line. They considered stationary engines, cable haulage, and horse power. To settle the question, they organised a competition for locomotives, held at Rainhill, near Liverpool, in October 1829. The trials were judged on a set of criteria, including weight, speed, the ability to pull a load, and reliability over a sustained run. Five entries were considered, and the rules required each engine to haul a train of a given weight over a set distance at an average speed that was demanding for the time.

Only four engines ran in the final trials. *Novelty*, built by John Ericsson and John Braithwaite, performed well but was not reliable. *Sans Pareil*, built by Hackworth, competed strongly but suffered problems in its later runs. *Perseverance*, a small engine, could not manage the required load. The winner was *Rocket*, built by George and Robert Stephenson with the assistance of Henry Booth, who proposed the multi-tube boiler that made the engine's steam generation effective. *Rocket* reached speeds of around thirty miles per hour in testing and pulled its load reliably. The prize of £500 was awarded, and the choice of steam locomotives was settled.

The line opened on 15 September 1830. The opening was marred by tragedy. William Huskisson, a Member of Parliament and a former cabinet minister, got out of his carriage on the track to speak with the Duke of Wellington, who was also on the train. *Rocket* was approaching on the adjacent track, and Huskisson was struck and fatally injured. The accident drew wide attention and was widely reported, but it did not diminish the line's commercial success. The Liverpool and Manchester carried passengers and freight quickly and regularly, and its timetable, speed, and reliability impressed observers. It became a model for railways in Britain and abroad.

The Liverpool and Manchester also established an important pattern. Its owners were business men who wanted returns on capital. Passenger receipts were significant, and the company ran trains of different classes at different prices. It used a double track, timetables, signals, and a system of management that foreshadowed the great railway companies that would emerge. The line's success persuaded many investors that railways were the coming form of transport.

## Gauge, Standards, and the Broad Gauge Quarrel

By the late 1830s, the British railway had settled on a gauge that would become universal. The Stephensons' lines, drawing on the practice of the north-eastern wagonways, used a track width of four feet eight and a half inches, or 1,435 millimetres. This gauge was not chosen by a scientific or national process. It was inherited from the colliery wagonways, where it had grown up because the wagons already had wheels of that spacing. Many early lines adopted it, partly because the Stephensons' engineering was so influential, and partly because the wagons and the locomotives of that gauge were readily available.

Isambard Kingdom Brunel, the engineer of the Great Western Railway, chose a different gauge. Brunel was a brilliant engineer with a strong sense of how a railway should ride, and he believed that a wider gauge would provide greater stability, more space for larger boilers, and smoother running at high speed. The GWR was authorised in 1835 and opened in stages from 1838. Its gauge was seven feet and a quarter of an inch, or 2,140 millimetres. Brunel's broad gauge lines ran a number of notably fast and comfortable trains, and the GWR earned a reputation for speed and smoothness. Daniel Gooch, the locomotive superintendent, built large engines to exploit the broad gauge, and some of them were remarkable for their time.

The result was a split. Broad gauge and standard gauge lines could not connect without transhipment, and this made the country's railway network awkward and expensive to use. Freight had to be unloaded and reloaded at breaks of gauge, and passengers had to change trains. The problem became serious as the network grew. Parliament appointed a Royal Commission in 1845 to examine the question. The commission's report, and the Gauge Act of 1846, decided in favour of the standard gauge for future lines. Broad gauge lines continued to operate for a time, but the GWR was gradually forced to convert its track. The last broad gauge trains ran in 1892, when the company completed the conversion of its remaining lines to standard gauge over a single weekend.

The gauge question shows something about how railways were built. Early standards were not set by national authorities but grew up through practice, commercial interest, and personal preference. When the network grew large enough, the lack of uniformity became expensive, and the state intervened to create a standard. This pattern would recur in other countries. Russia chose a broad gauge of 1,524 millimetres, partly for strategic reasons, and Spain and Portugal also chose wider gauges. Many countries in Latin America, Africa, and Asia adopted narrow or metre gauges to lower construction costs. Today's railways still bear the marks of these choices, and gauge remains one of the factors that makes international rail travel complicated.

## Railway Mania and the Shape of a Network

The years between 1844 and 1847 are known in Britain as the Railway Mania. The Liverpool and Manchester had demonstrated that railways could earn large returns, and investors rushed to subscribe to new companies. Hundreds of schemes were proposed, many of them speculative and some of them ill conceived. George Hudson, the "Railway King" of York, promoted a number of lines and used his position to build a financial empire. Hudson's companies were hugely profitable on paper for a time, but his methods involved questionable accounting and the distribution of dividends from capital, and when his schemes collapsed, many investors were ruined.

The mania led to the passage of important legislation. The Railway Regulation Act of 1844, introduced by William Ewart Gladstone when he was President of the Board of Trade, required railway companies to run at least one train a day with third-class accommodation at a fare of one penny a mile. The act also gave the state powers to inspect lines and to set certain standards, and it provided for the eventual purchase of railways by the state. Its effect was to make railways accessible to working people, and third-class travel became a major part of the business in the following decades. The mania also produced a great deal of construction. By the end of the period, Britain had a dense network of trunk lines and branches, and the main routes between major cities were in place.

The network's shape was governed by the economics of the period. Lines were built where traffic was expected to be heavy, and the companies competed fiercely for routes into large cities. Competing companies often built parallel lines, and some towns had multiple stations owned by different companies. Over time, the larger companies absorbed the smaller ones through amalgamation, and by the end of the nineteenth century Britain had a small number of major railway companies controlling most of the national network. The Railway Clearing House, established in 1842, organized the sharing of revenues from through traffic and made possible the carriage of a single ticket and a single consignment across several companies' lines. Its existence showed how much cooperation the system needed even when the companies were rivals.

Time was another consequence. Local time varied across Britain, and each town kept its own time based on the sun. Railways needed a uniform time to run timetables. The Great Western Railway adopted London time as its standard in 1840, and in 1847 the railway companies agreed to use Greenwich Mean Time across their networks. Over the following decades, the rest of the country gradually adopted it. The railways thus helped make Greenwich time the national standard, a change that affected daily life far beyond the railway itself.

## Spreading Across the World

The railway spread from Britain to the rest of the world with astonishing speed. The first lines on the European continent were built in the 1830s. In Belgium, the line from Brussels to Mechelen opened in 1835, and the Belgian state took an active role in planning and building its network, which made the country a model for continental railways. In Germany, the Ludwigsbahn between Nuremberg and Fürth opened in December 1835. It was a short line of a few kilometres, but it inaugurated the German railway age, and German states competed to build lines that would link their capitals and commercial centres. France had horse-drawn lines in the 1820s, and the line between Saint-Étienne and Lyon, opened in 1832, was a significant early steam-operated route. The French government was initially cautious about railways, but it later developed a national plan that led to the creation of a radial network centred on Paris.

The United States developed its railways in a different way. The country was vast, and the population was spread thinly across it. Railways were built by private companies, often with state or local government support, and the network grew through a combination of speculation and necessity. The Baltimore and Ohio, chartered in 1827, opened its first section in 1830. Its early engines included the *Tom Thumb*, a small experimental locomotive built by Peter Cooper, which famously lost a race against a horse when its belt slipped, though the locomotive was regarded as successful as a demonstration. American railways quickly adopted locomotives built in Britain and then developed their own designs, which were suited to the conditions of American lines: lighter track, steep grades in places, and a need for cheap construction. The first American locomotives often had a "cow catcher" at the front to deal with animals on the track, and their smokestacks were tall and spark-arresting.

The American network expanded rapidly. By the 1850s, several lines had reached the Mississippi and beyond. The Transcontinental Railroad, linking the eastern network to California, was completed in 1869 at Promontory Summit in Utah, with a famous ceremony in which the last spike was driven. Its construction involved enormous labour, including large numbers of Chinese and Irish workers, and it opened vast regions to settlement and trade. Canadian railways followed a similar pattern, and the Canadian Pacific Railway completed a transcontinental route in 1885, which was essential to the political unity of the Dominion.

Elsewhere, railways arrived as part of colonial and commercial expansion. In India, the first line, from Bombay to Thane, opened in April 1853, and the Indian railway network grew into one of the largest in the world. British engineers, capital, and locomotives dominated the early Indian railways, which were built partly to move troops and partly to serve the cotton and other export trades. In Australia, the first line in Victoria opened in 1854, and the colonies built separate networks that were later linked. South Africa's first railway opened in the Cape Colony in 1860. In South America, Argentina's first railway opened in 1857, and British capital funded many lines in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile, with the goods they carried often bound for export markets in Europe.

Russia's first line, from St Petersburg to Tsarskoye Selo, opened in 1837. The Russian government later built the great trunk routes that connected the capital with Moscow and other centres, and the Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in the 1890s, linked European Russia with the Pacific. Japan's first railway, from Shimbashi in Tokyo to Yokohama, opened in October 1872, with British help and British locomotives. The Japanese state built its network quickly and later established the great national railway system that would produce the Shinkansen. In China, the first railway, a short line in Shanghai called the Woosung Road, was built by British interests in 1876 and was purchased and removed by the Chinese government the following year, a dispute that reflects the tension between foreign capital and national sovereignty in the period. Chinese railways developed later, and by the early twentieth century they were a major part of the country's infrastructure.

The Ottoman Empire built the Hejaz Railway, which connected Damascus with Medina and was completed in 1908. Its purpose was partly religious, to make the pilgrimage to Mecca easier, and partly strategic, to tie the provinces of the empire more closely to Istanbul. It was damaged in the First World War and never reached Mecca. Its history illustrates the close relationship between railways, politics, and military power that characterized the period.

## Bridges, Tunnels, and the Engineering of Gradients

Railways made engineering a public spectacle. The problems of crossing rivers, valleys, and mountains were solved in ways that became famous. Robert Stephenson's Britannia Bridge, carrying the Chester and Holyhead line across the Menai Strait in north Wales, used wrought-iron tubes through which trains ran. The bridge was completed in 1850, and it was one of the first large structures built with wrought iron on this scale. Its design was tested and refined in response to a fire in the 1970s that damaged its decks, and it was later rebuilt with a steel arch. The Victoria Bridge in Montreal, completed in 1859, was a massive tubular bridge carrying a railway across the St Lawrence, and it was for many years one of the longest bridges in the world.

The viaduct became a characteristic railway structure. The Ribblehead Viaduct in Yorkshire, completed in 1874 for the Settle and Carlisle line, is a stone structure of many arches built across a wild moorland landscape, and its construction involved great hardship. Across Europe and the Americas, railway viaducts carried trains over rivers and valleys in spans of stone, iron, and later steel. The engineering of these structures reflected both practical necessity and the desire to impress, and many of them remain in use today.

Mountains presented the greatest challenge. Railways could handle gentle slopes, but steep gradients required either very powerful locomotives or special techniques. In the Alps, the Semmering Railway in Austria, designed by Carl von Ghega and completed in 1854, was one of the first major mountain railways in the world. It crossed the Semmering Pass, using a long series of viaducts and many tunnels, and it proved that a railway could climb steep terrain with reasonable curvature and gradient. Ghega's work set a standard for mountain railways and influenced later routes across the Alps.

Tunnels were another great achievement. The Mont Cenis Tunnel, between France and Italy, was opened in 1871 after a long construction period. It used rock drilling machines powered by compressed air, a technique that helped speed excavation and that was developed in response to the difficulties of the project. The Gotthard Tunnel in Switzerland, completed in 1882, was a major north-south link across the Alps, and it became a crucial route for European trade. Its opening was a significant event in the economic integration of northern and southern Europe.

Later tunnels pushed the scale further. The Simplon Tunnel, between Switzerland and Italy, was completed in 1906 and was for a time the longest tunnel in the world. The Seikan Tunnel, which opened in 1988 and runs under the Tsugaru Strait between Honshu and Hokkaido, is more than fifty kilometres long, with a significant undersea section. The Channel Tunnel, opened in 1994, connects England and France beneath the English Channel, with a total length of about fifty kilometres. The Gotthard Base Tunnel, opened in 2016, is the longest railway tunnel in the world at roughly fifty-seven kilometres, and it was designed to reduce gradients and allow faster trains through the Alps. These tunnels show how the engineering of railways has continued to depend on advances in tunnelling, drilling, ventilation, and geology.

Gradients were always a constraint, and railway engineers tried to keep them as gentle as possible because steep grades reduced the load a locomotive could pull and increased the strain on brakes and wheels. The result was a long history of route planning that accepted longer distances in exchange for easier climbs. Where the terrain was too severe, engineers used rack railways, cable systems, and special adhesion methods. The Mont Cenis line used a central rack system designed by John Barraclough Fell, and the Fell system was used on several other mountain lines. The Mount Washington Cog Railway in New Hampshire, opened in 1869, uses a rack system to climb a steep mountain. These specialized railways remain in service, and they serve as reminders that the railway was always adapting to the land it crossed.

## Locomotives Grow Up

The steam locomotive developed rapidly in the decades after *Rocket*. The early engines were small and light, with simple boilers, a single pair of driving wheels, and little capacity to haul large loads at speed. As traffic grew, designers needed more power, more stability, and more efficiency. The wheel arrangement became a standard way of classifying locomotives. Early engines were often 0-4-0 or 2-2-0, meaning the number of wheels in front, driven, and trailing positions. Designers added more driving wheels to increase adhesion and pulling power, and they added leading and trailing wheels to improve stability at speed. The American 4-4-0 "American" type became widely used in the United States, while the British built engines with a variety of wheel arrangements suited to their own lines.

Boiler design improved steadily. The multi-tube boiler introduced for *Rocket* allowed more heating surface and faster steam generation, and later designers refined the principle. Superheating, which heats steam beyond its saturation point, was developed in the late nineteenth century and was widely adopted in the early twentieth. It improved the efficiency of steam engines and reduced water consumption. Compounding, in which steam expands through two cylinders in sequence, was another improvement, and the Mallet articulated locomotive, which divided its driving wheels into two sets on separate frames, allowed very large engines to negotiate curves. Mallets were used on heavy freight lines in the United States, Europe, and Africa, and they were among the largest steam locomotives ever built.

Passenger locomotives became fast and elegant. The 4-4-2 "Atlantic" type, developed in the United States and widely used in Britain and Europe, was designed for fast express trains. The 4-6-2 "Pacific" type, with a larger firebox and a leading bogie, became the standard for high-speed passenger work in the early twentieth century. In Britain, the London and North Western and the Great Western built fast locomotives that set records and carried famous express trains such as the Flying Scotsman. The Pennsylvania Railroad's streamlined K4s Pacific of the 1930s, and the French and German steam locomotives of the interwar years, pushed steam to remarkable performance. André Chapelon, a French engineer, applied a series of improvements to the steam locomotive in the 1930s and 1940s, including improved steam passages and exhaust design, and his work showed that steam still had room for development when most people thought it was obsolete.

The largest steam locomotives were built for freight in the United States. The Union Pacific's Big Boy, a 4-8-8-4 articulated locomotive built in the early 1940s, was one of the largest and most powerful steam engines ever constructed. It was built to haul heavy freight over the mountains of Wyoming and Utah. Its scale reflected the demands of American freight traffic and the availability of fuel and materials. These great machines were a culmination of a century of development, and they were soon to be overtaken by a different form of power.

Steam locomotives were also complicated to maintain. They needed coal or oil, water, ash removal, boiler inspection, and frequent servicing. They produced smoke and cinders, and their efficiency was limited by the thermodynamics of the steam cycle. Crews worked in difficult conditions, and the work of firing, driving, and maintaining locomotives was demanding and dangerous. The social culture of the steam railway, with its distinctive trades and loyalties, shaped the lives of many workers, and the decline of steam would bring large changes to those communities.

## Carrying People

The railway transformed travel. Before railways, long-distance journeys in Britain relied on stagecoaches, which were slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. The railway offered faster and cheaper travel, and it opened the possibility of day trips, holidays, and commuting. Early railways classified passengers into first, second, and third class, with different levels of comfort and fares. First-class carriages were upholstered and private, while third-class passengers often travelled in open wagons or simple benches. The Railway Regulation Act of 1844 required third-class accommodation on certain trains, and the third-class passenger became a major part of the railway's business.

Thomas Cook, a Leicester businessman, organized one of the first commercial railway excursions in 1841, carrying temperance supporters to a meeting. The idea of the package excursion grew from this experiment, and Cook's company developed into a travel agency that organized tours across Britain and the world. The railway made the seaside resort, the spa, and the holiday destination accessible to ordinary people, and it helped create the modern concept of leisure travel.

Long-distance comfort improved steadily. The sleeping car was developed in the United States in the 1860s, and George Pullman built sleeping cars that became famous for their luxury. The Pioneer, built in 1864, was an early Pullman sleeper, and Pullman's company went on to build many cars for American railroads. The sleeper transformed long-distance journeys, allowing passengers to travel overnight in reasonable comfort. The dining car, introduced in the late nineteenth century, allowed passengers to eat during their journey, and it became a symbol of the railway's refinement. European sleeping cars, such as those on the Orient Express, which began running in 1883, offered luxury travel across the continent. The Orient Express became a byword for glamour and intrigue in literature and film.

The railway also changed how people thought about time, distance, and the nation. Timetables made travel predictable, and station clocks became a common feature of urban life. The railway station became a central part of the city, a place of arrival and departure, and it was often built as a monumental structure that expressed the confidence of the company that owned it. Stations such as St Pancras in London, Grand Central Terminal in New York, and the Gare de Lyon in Paris are examples of this architecture, and they reflect the importance of the railway to the modern city.

Commuting developed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Suburban railways allowed people to live outside the crowded city centres and travel to work by train. This pattern shaped the growth of suburbs around London, Paris, New York, Berlin, and other cities. The commuter train became a daily routine for millions of workers, and the railway timetable structured the working day. In many cities, the suburban railway was the first form of mass transit, and it remains central to urban transport today.

## Carrying Goods

Freight was the railway's original purpose and remained its economic foundation for a century and more. Coal, iron, grain, timber, and manufactured goods moved by rail in quantities that no road or canal could match. The railway's advantage was its combination of speed, capacity, and regularity. A single train could carry hundreds of tons, and a locomotive could pull a long string of wagons over distance, with a predictable schedule. The railway made possible the concentration of industry around coalfields and ports, and it enabled the supply of cities with food and raw materials on a scale that had not been possible before.

Freight was organized through wagon load traffic, in which individual shippers sent goods in wagons that might be combined into trains at marshalling yards. Marshalling yards, where wagons were sorted and assembled into trains, were some of the most complex and labour-intensive places in the railway. The hump yard, in which wagons were pushed over a hump and rolled down into sidings, was developed in the late nineteenth century and became common in the twentieth. The hump yard allowed faster sorting of wagons, but it required careful brakes and signals, and it was dangerous work.

Specialized freight services developed. Refrigerated wagons carried meat, fish, and perishable produce, and the refrigerated railway wagon made it possible to ship food from Argentina, Australia, and the American West to distant markets. Tank wagons carried oil and chemicals, and hopper wagons carried coal, ore, and grain. The development of bulk freight was a major part of the railway's business in the twentieth century, and many lines were built or upgraded to serve heavy industry.

The railway also gave rise to the concept of through freight. Goods could be sent from one part of the country to another under a single contract, and the railway companies cooperated to make this possible. Container traffic was an important development in the twentieth century. Standard containers, which could be moved between ships, trains, and trucks without unloading their contents, were developed in the 1950s and 1960s, and they transformed the shipping and freight industries. The intermodal container allowed the railway to compete for long-distance freight on a new basis, though it also tied railways more closely to ports and road networks.

The railway's freight business was affected by road transport from the 1920s onward. Motor lorries and buses offered door-to-door service and flexibility that railways could not easily match. For short distances, road haulage was often faster and cheaper, and as road networks improved and motor vehicles became more reliable, they took a growing share of the freight market. In Britain, the railway companies faced severe competition after the Second World War, and the nationalised British Railways struggled to adapt. In the United States, the post-war growth of trucking and the expansion of the highway network eroded railway freight, and several major railroads went into financial distress. Penn Central, formed by the merger of the Pennsylvania and New York Central railroads, went bankrupt in 1970, and the federal government stepped in to create Conrail to take over the bankrupt lines in the Northeast.

The American response, the Staggers Rail Act of 1980, deregulated the railroads, allowing them to set rates, abandon unprofitable lines, and make contracts with shippers. The act helped the freight railroads recover, and by the late twentieth century American freight railways were among the most efficient in the world, carrying large volumes of coal, grain, chemicals, and intermodal containers. The American experience shows that freight railways could survive and even thrive when they were freed from certain regulatory constraints, though the railway industry remained sensitive to changes in fuel prices, trade patterns, and the state of the economy.

## Electricity

The electric railway had its origins in experiments of the 1830s and 1840s, when inventors built small electric locomotives powered by batteries. These early machines were impractical for commercial service, because batteries were heavy and expensive and the electric motor was not yet well developed. The decisive advance came with the development of the dynamo, which could generate electricity mechanically in quantities suitable for industrial use. In 1879, Werner von Siemens exhibited an electric railway at the Berlin Trade Exhibition, a small train pulled by an electric locomotive and powered by a generator through a central rail. The first electric tramway to carry passengers in regular service was built by Siemens and Halske at Berlin-Lichterfelde in 1881, and it was an important demonstration that electric traction could carry people in everyday use.

Magnus Volk, an English engineer, built the Volk's Electric Railway at Brighton in 1883, a seafront line that still operates and is often described as the oldest operating electric railway in the world. Its success helped persuade engineers that electric traction was practical for urban and seaside railways. Electric trams spread quickly through the cities of Europe and North America in the 1880s and 1890s. The trams used overhead wires with trolley poles or pantographs, or in some cases conduit systems in which the power was supplied through a slot in the road. The electric tram transformed urban transport, allowing faster and cheaper movement within cities and enabling the growth of suburbs.

Main-line electrification developed more slowly. The problems of high-voltage supply, reliable motors, and safe overhead equipment were significant. The Baltimore and Ohio built electric locomotives for a tunnel in Baltimore in 1895, and the New York Central electrified its approaches to Grand Central Terminal in the first decade of the twentieth century. The Pennsylvania Railroad built a large electrified system in New York, including the tunnels under the Hudson River, which opened in the early twentieth century. These projects showed that electrification could work on heavy lines, though the economics were difficult.

European countries were also developing electric systems. In Italy, the Valtellina line used three-phase alternating current in 1902, and the three-phase system was used on several Italian and Swiss routes in the early years of the century. The Swiss Federal Railways and other railways in the Alps adopted electrification because hydroelectric power was abundant and steam locomotives struggled with long tunnels and steep grades. Electrification also had obvious environmental and operating advantages in tunnels, where smoke and steam were hazards to crews and passengers.

The electric locomotive gave railways greater power, faster acceleration, and reduced maintenance compared with steam. Electric traction also made it possible to recover energy through regenerative braking, which allowed trains to return power to the supply when slowing down. Electric systems were expensive to build because they required substations, overhead wires or third rails, and specialized vehicles. Their economic justification depended on heavy traffic and the availability of cheap electricity. Over the twentieth century, many countries electrified their busiest routes, especially in Europe, Japan, and the northeastern United States.

The electrification of railways also reshaped the relationship between railways and power generation. Railways began to rely on utilities and national grids, and they became large consumers of electricity. In some countries, the state built hydroelectric plants to supply railways, and the railway became part of a national energy infrastructure. This history shows that the railway's future depended not only on engineering but also on energy policy.

## Diesel and the Long Retreat from Steam

The diesel engine, patented by Rudolf Diesel in the 1890s, offered high efficiency and the ability to run on heavy oil. Diesel engines were first applied to road vehicles and ships, and then to railways. Early diesel locomotives were built in the 1910s and 1920s, and the Swiss firm Winterthur built one of the first successful diesel-electric locomotives in 1912. Diesel-electric transmission, in which a diesel engine drives a generator that powers electric traction motors, became the most practical form of diesel railway traction. It avoided the complexity of mechanical gearboxes and allowed the engine to run at its most efficient speed.

In the United States, the Electro-Motive Division of General Motors developed diesel-electric locomotives in the 1930s. The Burlington and Santa Fe railroads bought diesel passenger locomotives, and the success of the diesel-electric in passenger service persuaded other railroads to consider it. The Electro-Motive FT locomotive, introduced in 1939, was a major success, and its design was built in large numbers after the Second World War. Diesel traction was far cheaper to maintain than steam, required less labour, and could operate for longer periods without servicing. Diesels did not need water or coal, which simplified operations at remote locations.

The transition from steam to diesel was one of the most profound changes in railway history. In the United States, the great majority of steam locomotives were retired by the 1950s, and by about 1960 the railroads were almost entirely diesel. In Britain, the British Railways Modernisation Plan of 1955 set out to replace steam with diesel and electric traction, and the last steam locomotives in regular service were withdrawn in 1968. Other countries followed at different speeds, and some, such as South Africa, India, and China, kept steam for longer periods. In many countries, steam locomotives became historical objects, preserved by enthusiasts and museums, and steam excursions became a popular form of heritage travel.

The end of steam had social consequences. Engine sheds and locomotive works closed, and many workers lost jobs in communities built around railway operations. The distinctive craft skills of firemen, drivers, and fitters were no longer needed in the same way. Diesel and electric locomotives required different skills, and the railway workforce was reorganised accordingly. The change also affected the landscape, as railway works and sheds were removed or repurposed, and the railway's visual character changed from the smoke and steam of the steam age to the cleaner profile of the diesel and electric train.

Diesel traction was a relatively short-lived answer to the question of railway power. It has been widely replaced on main lines by electric traction, which offers lower operating costs and cleaner operation in places where electricity is readily available. Diesel remains important on lines without electrification, especially in the United States, Australia, and parts of Africa and Asia. Its economic and environmental advantages have made it a central part of railway operation for much of the twentieth century, and its legacy is visible in the locomotives still in service today.

## Nationalisation, Privatisation, and Regulation

The railway has always been a political question. Its construction required large amounts of capital, its operation affected the public, and its monopolies raised concerns about fares and service. Governments intervened in railways from early on, through legislation, inspection, and regulation. In Britain, the railway was dominated by private companies until the First World War, when the state took control of the railways for the war effort. The Railways Act of 1921 grouped the companies into four large regional railways, the so-called Big Four, which operated until nationalisation.

The Second World War placed further strain on the railways, and they were nationalised in 1948, when the newly created British Railways took over the lines and the operation of the network. Nationalisation was part of a broader political programme of state ownership in the post-war period, and it was intended to bring coordinated planning and investment to a fragmented system. The British Railways Modernisation Plan of 1955 was a major attempt to renew the system, but the scale of the task and the economic difficulties of the period made progress uneven.

The Beeching Report of 1963, *The Reshaping of British Railways*, proposed the closure of many lightly used lines and stations. Its recommendations were controversial, and they led to the closure of thousands of miles of track and hundreds of stations over the following decade. The Beeching cuts became a symbol of the decline of rural railways in Britain, and their legacy is still debated. Some closed lines have since been reopened, and the debate over the appropriate role of railways in low-density areas continues.

Britain privatised its railways in the 1990s. The Railways Act of 1993 separated the infrastructure from operations, creating a system of franchised passenger services and private freight operators, while the track and stations were owned by Railtrack, a private company. The privatisation was controversial, and the structure created complex relationships between infrastructure and operators. Railtrack went into administration in 2001 after a series of accidents and maintenance failures, notably the Hatfield crash in 2000, and its functions were transferred to Network Rail, a not-for-profit company owned by the state. The British experience shows how difficult it is to separate and regulate railway functions, and it has prompted continuing debate about the best structure for the industry.

Japan took a different path. The Japanese National Railways were privatised in 1987, and the system was divided into six regional passenger companies and a freight company. The Japan Railways companies, known as JR, operated their own networks, and the privatisation helped reduce the large deficits that had accumulated under state ownership. The new companies were able to develop their own businesses, including real estate, retail, and tourism, and the JR system became profitable in several cases. The Japanese model combined regional competition with a national standard for service and safety, and it has been widely studied as an example of successful reform.

Other countries retained public ownership. Germany's Deutsche Bahn was formed from the combination of the West and East German railways in 1994, and it remains a state-owned company, though it has undergone several reforms and internal reorganisations. France's SNCF is also state-owned, and it operates both the national network and the high-speed services. Russia's railways are run by a state-owned company, and China's railways are operated by the China State Railway Group, which oversees a vast network. The variety of ownership models reflects different political traditions and different judgments about the role of the state in infrastructure.

Regulation has also changed. Railway safety regimes have been strengthened in response to accidents, and many countries have established independent regulators to oversee safety, competition, and access to networks. The European Union has pursued a series of railway packages aimed at opening national markets to competition and creating interoperable systems across borders. These measures have had mixed results, but they reflect the growing importance of cross-border rail travel and freight in the European economy.

## The Shinkansen and the Speed Revolution

The Shinkansen, the Japanese high-speed railway, opened on 1 October 1964, when the first trains began running on the Tokaido line between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka. The line was 515 kilometres long, and its trains were designed to run at 210 kilometres per hour, a speed that was unprecedented for a commercially operated railway. The line was built to standard gauge, not the narrow gauge used on many Japanese lines, and it was a separate network of dedicated tracks, with signals, safety systems, and power supply designed for high speed. The Tokaido Shinkansen was built in advance of the Tokyo Olympics of 1964, and its opening was a symbol of Japan's recovery and modernity after the Second World War.

The engineering of the Shinkansen was an achievement. The line needed a track with very smooth geometry, large radius curves, and tight tolerances. Its trains had streamlined noses, pantographs for overhead electric supply, and aerodynamic designs that reduced noise and drag. The line was signalled by an automatic system, and its operations were controlled from a central office. Its reliability and safety record became legendary, and for more than half a century, no passenger has died in an accident on the line. This record is attributed to careful design, rigorous maintenance, a strict operating culture, and an emphasis on punctuality.

The Shinkansen changed Japanese life. It cut the journey time between Tokyo and Osaka from about six hours to around three, and later it was reduced further. The line allowed the growth of business travel between the country's largest cities, and it helped concentrate economic activity along the corridor. Its success prompted the construction of new lines across Japan, extending the network to the north and west. The network today includes several lines radiating from Tokyo, and the trains operate at speeds of up to 320 kilometres per hour on some sections.

The Shinkansen also influenced railway planning worldwide. Other countries studied its operations, and many of its principles were adopted in later systems. The Japanese experience showed that high-speed rail could be commercially viable in dense corridors, that it could be operated safely at high speed, and that it could attract passengers away from aviation and road travel on routes of a few hundred kilometres. It also demonstrated that a railway could be a symbol of national achievement and that the design of a train could express the identity of a nation.

Japan's high-speed network has had some costs. The construction of lines through mountainous terrain required large numbers of tunnels and viaducts, and the expense was considerable. The network's finances have been supported by a combination of fares, real estate development, and public investment. Some lines have been criticised for their cost or for their limited use, but the overall network remains one of the most successful examples of high-speed rail in the world.

## Speed Records, Maglev, and the Frontier

The French TGV, or Train à Grande Vitesse, was the second major high-speed system to enter service. Its first commercial service, between Paris and Lyon, began on 27 September 1981, using a line built specially for high-speed operation. The TGV ran at speeds of up to 270 kilometres per hour on the new line, and it used tilting and articulated designs that reduced weight and improved stability. The TGV was designed by a team of French engineers and was built by a consortium of French manufacturers, and it became a symbol of French technological ambition.

The TGV set a series of speed records. On 18 May 1990, a TGV Atlantique set a record of 515.3 kilometres per hour on a test run, a figure that stood for many years as the speed record for conventional wheel-on-rail trains. In 2007, a modified French train, the V150, reached 574.8 kilometres per hour on a test run, the highest speed ever recorded by a conventional railway train. These records were achieved under special test conditions, but they demonstrated the potential of wheel-on-rail technology at speeds far beyond the normal operating range.

High-speed rail spread through Europe. Germany's Intercity-Express, or ICE, entered service in 1991, after the opening of the Hanover to Würzburg line, which was designed for high speed. The ICE used a different design from the TGV, and it operated over a combination of new and existing lines. Italy developed a high-speed line between Rome and Florence, known as the Direttissima, which opened in 1977 and was among the first lines in Europe designed for speeds above 200 kilometres per hour. Spain opened its high-speed line between Madrid and Seville in 1992, in time for the Seville Expo, and the Spanish AVE network has since grown into one of the largest in Europe. The Eurostar service, opened in 1994 with the Channel Tunnel, connected London with Paris and Brussels, and it showed that high-speed rail could cross national borders and compete with air travel.

Maglev, or magnetic levitation, was another line of development. Maglev trains float above their guideway and are propelled by electromagnetic forces, eliminating wheel-rail contact and allowing very high speeds. The German Transrapid system was developed in the 1970s and 1980s, and a commercial line was built in Shanghai, opened in 2004, connecting Pudong airport with the city. The Shanghai Maglev reaches speeds of up to 431 kilometres per hour, though its commercial operation covers a relatively short distance. The Japanese SCMaglev, developed by Central Japan Railway, uses superconducting magnets and has been tested at speeds above 600 kilometres per hour in the Yamanashi test line. Japan has planned a maglev line between Tokyo and Nagoya, with later extension to Osaka, but the project has been delayed by costs, tunnelling challenges, and environmental concerns.

The maglev has so far remained a niche technology. Its advantage is speed, and its disadvantages include high cost, the need for a dedicated guideway, and limited compatibility with existing railway networks. It has attracted interest because it promises very high speeds, but its practical use has been limited. The dispute between maglev and conventional high-speed rail reflects a broader question about how the railway should develop in the future: whether to extend wheel-on-rail technology, which is compatible with existing networks, or to invest in new systems that promise higher speeds and different operating characteristics.

The frontier of railway speed remains contested. Engineers have continued to explore higher speeds for wheel-on-rail trains, and the limits of adhesion, aerodynamic drag, and track wear constrain the top speeds of commercial services. Most high-speed lines operate at speeds between 250 and 350 kilometres per hour, a range that balances speed, energy use, and infrastructure cost. The debate continues about whether faster speeds are worth their expense, and the answer depends on the density of travel demand, the availability of alternative modes, and the political priorities of the countries concerned.

## High-Speed Rail Today and Its Problems

High-speed rail today is a significant part of the transport system in several countries. China has built the largest high-speed network in the world, beginning with the Beijing to Tianjin line, which opened in 2008 and was designed for speeds of 350 kilometres per hour. The Chinese network expanded rapidly over the following years, and by the mid-2020s it included more than forty thousand kilometres of high-speed track. The network has connected many of the country's major cities and has reshaped travel patterns across the country. Chinese high-speed trains are built by domestic manufacturers, and their development has been a major part of China's industrial policy. The rapid expansion has also raised questions about cost, debt, and the financial sustainability of the system, and some lines carry relatively few passengers.

Europe's high-speed network is extensive, though it is a patchwork of national systems. Germany, France, Spain, Italy, and other countries have built lines that connect their major cities, and cross-border services have been developed where possible. The integration of European high-speed rail has been slow, because national operators, different signalling systems, and different electrical standards create technical and administrative barriers. The European Union has promoted interoperability and the development of cross-border routes, but progress has been uneven, and air travel remains competitive on many long-distance routes.

The United States has been slower to develop high-speed rail. The Northeast Corridor between Boston, New York, and Washington has carried fast trains for many years, and the Acela service operates at speeds of up to around 150 miles per hour on short sections, though much of the route is limited by curves, tunnels, and the age of its infrastructure. Plans for a larger high-speed network have been proposed and debated for decades, and several projects, such as the California High-Speed Rail project, have faced large cost increases, legal disputes, and political opposition. The American experience shows how difficult it can be to build high-speed rail in a country with a dispersed population, a strong automobile culture, and a complicated system of government.

The United Kingdom's High Speed 2 project, intended to connect London with the Midlands and the north, has also faced large cost increases and delays. The project was approved in principle in the 2010s, and construction began in the 2020s, but its scope was reduced and its timetable extended, and its future has been the subject of political debate. The British experience illustrates a common problem with large railway projects: their costs and benefits depend on long-term forecasts, and their political support can change over the life of the construction.

High-speed rail also raises environmental questions. Its construction requires large amounts of land, concrete, and steel, and it can disrupt communities and ecosystems. Its operation uses electricity, and its carbon footprint depends on the source of that electricity. Compared with aviation, high-speed rail generally has lower emissions per passenger kilometre, and it can reduce the need for short-haul flights and car journeys. These advantages have made high-speed rail a popular part of climate policy in several countries, though its benefits depend on how it is used and whether it attracts passengers from other modes.

Freight, passenger, and urban rail continue to evolve. Metro systems, light rail, and commuter networks have expanded in many cities, and some have adopted driverless operation and advanced signalling. Freight railways are adapting to new supply chains, decarbonisation pressures, and digital technology. Battery-electric and hydrogen trains are being developed for lines where full electrification is impractical, and some countries have begun to operate them. Digital signalling, automatic train operation, and data-driven maintenance are changing how railways are managed and how capacity is used.

The history of railways is a history of technical ingenuity responding to economic and political demands. The wooden rails of the mines, the iron tramroads of the industrial revolution, the steam locomotives of the nineteenth century, the electric and diesel traction of the twentieth, and the high-speed trains of the present all reflect a continuing effort to move people and goods more efficiently across land. Each stage has been shaped by the materials available, the capital that could be raised, the politics of the time, and the demands of the people who used the railway. The railway has been both a cause and a consequence of change: it reshaped cities, economies, and national identities, and it was reshaped in turn by the forces it helped unleash. Its story, from a horse pulling a cart along a timber track to a train running at more than three hundred kilometres per hour, is one of steady invention and persistent adaptation.
